title: Ratio & Proportion
shortDescription: Divide by the SUM of ratio parts, not by one term — the single habit that fixes most ratio-distribution mistakes.
genZNote: A ratio is just a fraction that refuses to simplify itself. You do that part — find 'one part' by dividing by the total, then scale up.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: A ratio a:b compares two quantities of the SAME kind. A proportion states two ratios are equal (a:b = c:d), which cross-multiplies to ad = bc. The one habit that prevents almost every ratio-distribution mistake: when splitting a total in a given ratio, divide the TOTAL by the SUM of the ratio parts first to find the value of 'one part', then multiply by each individual part.

sections.heading: Dividing a Total in a Given Ratio

steps.name: Standard method
steps.explanation: Split ₹600 in the ratio 2:3:5. Sum of parts = 2+3+5 = 10. Value of one part = 600/10 = 60.

steps.name: Fast method
steps.explanation: Multiply the unit value by each ratio term directly: 2×60=120, 3×60=180, 5×60=300 — check they sum back to 600 as a fast self-check.
steps.purpose: The sum-back check catches arithmetic slips in seconds, before submitting an answer.

sections.heading: Cross-Multiplication for Unknown Terms
sections.body: If a:b = c:d, then ad = bc. Use this directly to solve for a missing term in a proportion rather than converting both sides to decimals first.

sections.heading: Compound Ratios & Comparing Ratios
bullets: Compound ratio: multiply corresponding terms of two or more ratios together, e.g. (a:b) compounded with (c:d) = ac:bd.
To compare two ratios quickly (e.g. is 3:4 bigger or smaller than 5:7?), cross-multiply: 3×7=21 vs 4×5=20 — since 21>20, 3:4 > 5:7. Faster than converting both to decimals.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Dividing the total directly by one ratio term instead of by the SUM of all ratio terms first.
Forgetting to simplify a ratio to lowest terms before comparing it against another — an unsimplified ratio can look bigger or smaller than it actually is at a glance.
Mixing up units on the two sides of a ratio — a ratio only compares like quantities in the same unit.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Always find the value of 'one part' (total ÷ sum of parts) before computing individual shares.
Use cross-multiplication to compare or solve ratios instead of converting to decimals, especially with fractions.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: A ratio compares like quantities; dividing a total in a ratio means dividing by the SUM of the parts first, then scaling.
keyFacts: One part = Total ÷ (sum of ratio terms).

Compare ratios fast via cross-multiplication instead of converting to decimals.
commonConfusion: Dividing a total by one ratio term instead of by the sum of all terms is the single most common ratio-distribution error.
